lessons.title: Zentangle patterns and strings
objectives: Divide a page with 'strings' into sections
Fill sections with at least four different patterns

keywords.def: a relaxing drawing method using structured repeating patterns
a repeated design or decoration
art that does not try to look realistic
how shapes and patterns are arranged on the page
a line that divides the page into sections to fill

teach.heading: What is Zentangle?
bullets: A relaxing way to draw patterns
Developed by Rick Roberts and Maria Thomas
Slow, repeated strokes build a design
teach.note: Show examples of tangles. Link to calm and focus (wellbeing). Pupils need a pencil, a black ink pen, paper. From the school's Y9 lesson plan: previous knowledge is Zentangle patterns.

teach.heading: Strings and sections
bullets: Draw light pencil lines across the page
Each section gets its own pattern
teach.note: Model a curved string splitting a square into five. Misconception: you need to plan every pattern; just begin.

teach.heading: Simple patterns
teach.note: Teach three tangles step by step: a grid of dots, scales (overlapping arcs), and stripes. Copy into books, as the plan says.

teach.heading: Optical illusion patterns
teach.note: Bridget Riley is a British artist known for Op Art. Show a checkerboard that bulges. Ask: how does it trick the eye?

teach.heading: Make your own page
teach.note: Differentiate: easy patterns for some, medium and higher for others. Keep lines clean; do not rush.

practice: What is a string in Zentangle?
How does Op Art trick the eye?
independent: Draw three tangles in boxes: dots grid, scales, stripes.
Add shading to one tangle to make it look 3D.
exit: Fill a page divided by strings with at least four different patterns.
lessons.send: Create three new patterns in your sketchbook and shade them.

lessons.title: Abstract leaf: composition and mark-making
objectives: Apply patterns and optical illusions to sections
Experiment with mark-making using household items

keywords.def: art that does not try to look realistic
how shapes and patterns are arranged on the page
creating lines, textures or prints using different tools
an area of the page filled with its own pattern

starter: How can you make a pattern look 3D?

teach.heading: The final project
bullets: An abstract leaf filled with patterns
Not realistic, only shapes and patterns
Show the Zentangle and Op Art ideas
teach.note: Show an example. Explain abstract: a leaf shape is a way to arrange patterns; the outline is only a starting point. Pupils need a black ink pen, pencil, paper (a large card is fine).

teach.heading: Planning the composition
teach.note: Model a simple outline. Ask: where is your pattern densest? Balance dark and light.

teach.heading: Filling with patterns
teach.note: Pupils choose their level; teacher moves between them. Remind: a clear, careful line is better than a rushed busy one.

teach.heading: Mark-making with household items
bullets: Dip lightly in paint or ink
teach.note: Ask a grown-up to help. Pupils may use pencil shading or dotted marks if paint is unavailable. Protect the table with newspaper; wash hands afterwards.

teach.heading: Showing our work
teach.note: Add to a class virtual art wall. Best pupil explains how they did it.

practice: Name one thing used for mark-making.
How can a leaf be abstract?
independent: Draw and divide a leaf outline into at least six sections.
Fill two sections with different patterns.
exit: Complete your abstract leaf with at least six patterns and one mark-making texture.
Write two sentences evaluating your composition.
homework: Which pattern is your best and why?
lessons.send: Finish your leaf and add shading to three sections.

lessons.title: What is optical illusion art?
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you trust your eyes? Two lines can be exactly the same length and still look different. How?
objectives: To understand how optical illusion (Op) art tricks the eye using line, shape and contrast
successCriteria: All: describe what an optical illusion is
Most: explain how one illusion works (pattern, contrast or perspective)
Some: make a simple illusion and explain the trick it uses
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: how the eye and brain process light
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: humility about the limits of our senses

keywords.def: an image that tricks the eye into seeing something that is not there
a 1960s art movement using illusions of movement and depth
a strong difference, such as black against white
a repeated design

hook.text: Can you trust your eyes? Two lines can be exactly the same length and still look different. How?
hook.a: The brain uses clues (arrows, angles) to judge size; illusions exploit those clues.

islamicLink.text: Our senses are a blessing and also limited. Allah says that hearing, sight and the heart will all be questioned (al-Isra 17:36), reminding us to use them carefully and check before we judge. Illusions show how easily the eye can be misled.

starter.a: Colours opposite on the colour wheel.
Drawing depth with lines meeting at one vanishing point.

teach.heading: Illusions trick the brain
bullets: The eye sees, the brain interprets
teach.note: Show the Müller-Lyer lines: measure them live with a ruler.

teach.heading: Types of illusion
teach.note: Show each as a diagram.

teach.heading: Op art
bullets: Black and white lines that seem to move
teach.note: Abstract and geometric: no figures, a good fit for our art rules.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: In the Müller-Lyer illusion the two lines are...
check.why: They are equal; the arrow ends make the brain misjudge them.

practice.q: Draw the Müller-Lyer illusion with two 6 cm lines. Measure to prove they are equal.
practice.a: Two 6 cm lines, one with outward and one with inward arrowheads.
practice.model: Teacher rules two 6 cm lines, adds arrowheads, then measures both on camera.

practice.q: Name the trick in the Penrose triangle.
practice.a: It is an impossible object: each corner looks correct but the whole cannot exist in 3D.

independent.q: Core: Copy three simple illusions (Müller-Lyer, café wall, Penrose triangle) neatly with a ruler on one page.
independent.model: Teacher starts the café wall: rows of black and white squares, each row shifted half a square.

independent.q: Extend: Under each, write in one sentence how it tricks the eye.
independent.a: Arrows mislead length; shifted rows make parallel lines look sloped; corners combine impossibly.

independent.q: Stretch: Invent a small illusion of your own and explain the trick in the portal response box.
independent.a: Any illusion with a clear explanation.

exit.q: Op art is known for... A) portraits B) illusions of movement with lines and contrast C) landscapes
exit.a: B) illusions of movement with lines and contrast
options: Illusions of movement with lines and contrast

exit.q: Big question: can we always trust our eyes? Give an example.
exit.a: No: the Müller-Lyer lines look different but are the same length.

lessons.homework: Find one optical illusion in everyday life (a floor pattern, a road marking) and photograph or sketch it.
lessons.send: SEND: dotted templates to complete. EAL: illusion, contrast, pattern. Stretch: research Bridget Riley's use of black and white.
resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary Creative Arts five-year scheme of work (optical illusion half term) and Art & Design Curriculum Intent, Year 9
At home: sketchbook or A4 paper, ruler, pencils (HB, 2B), compass or round objects to draw around, black fine liner, coloured pencils or felt tips
Illusions reference sheet (pupil PDF)

lessons.title: 3D drawing revisited: shading for depth
lessons.bigQuestion: A flat square becomes a cube with just three lines and some shading. What makes us believe it?
objectives: To understand how tone and perspective make flat shapes appear three-dimensional
successCriteria: All: draw a cube in two-point perspective
Most: shade three faces with three different tones from one light direction
Some: shade a curved form (a cylinder or sphere) with a smooth gradient
lessons.smsc: Moral: precision and care in technical drawing

keywords.def: having height, width and depth
drawing depth with lines that meet at vanishing points
a smooth change from light to dark
where the light comes from

hook.text: A flat square becomes a cube with just three lines and some shading. What makes us believe it?
hook.a: Perspective lines and three tones tell the brain there are three faces at different angles to the light.

starter.a: An image that tricks the eye.
options: An image that tricks the eye

starter.q: Name the line where vanishing points sit.
How many vanishing points in two-point perspective?
Where does a cast shadow fall?

teach.heading: Cubes in two-point perspective
bullets: Horizon line with two vanishing points
Join top and bottom to both points
teach.note: Recap of two-point perspective; model it fully for pupils new to it.

teach.heading: Three faces, three tones
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Shade a cube lit from the top left.
steps: Top face: lightest, leave almost white
Right face: darkest; cast shadow to the right

teach.heading: Curved forms
teach.note: Show the difference between flat and curved shading.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Light comes from the top. Which face of a cube is lightest?
check.why: The face facing the light receives most light.

practice.q: Draw a cube in two-point perspective and shade its three faces.
practice.a: Light, mid and dark faces with a cast shadow.
practice.model: Teacher draws the horizon, two points, the near edge, then shades from the model slide.

independent.q: Core: Draw a group of three boxes of different sizes in two-point perspective, all shaded from the same light.
independent.a: Three consistent shaded boxes with cast shadows.

independent.q: Extend: Add a shaded cylinder to the group.
independent.a: A cylinder with a smooth vertical gradient.

independent.q: Stretch: Add a floating box: how does its cast shadow change?
independent.a: The shadow is further from the box and lighter or softer.

exit.q: A smooth change from light to dark is a... A) gradient B) horizon C) vanishing point
exit.a: A) gradient

exit.q: Big question: what makes a flat drawing look 3D?
exit.a: Perspective lines and tones that follow one light source.

lessons.homework: Shade a real box (a cereal box) from life with one lamp as the light source.
lessons.send: SEND: a cube template to shade. EAL: face, light, dark, shadow. Stretch: three-point perspective tower.

lessons.title: Line-based illusions: curved lines and warped grids
lessons.bigQuestion: How can straight lines on flat paper make it look as if a ball is pushing up through the page?
objectives: To understand how bending a regular grid with lines creates the illusion of a swelling or sinking surface
successCriteria: All: draw an even grid of lines
Most: curve the lines around a shape to make a bulge
Some: alternate black and white so the bulge appears to move or rise
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: contour lines on maps show hills by line spacing
lessons.smsc: Cultural: line rhythm in Op art and in Islamic architectural patterns

keywords.def: a pattern of crossing lines in rows and columns
bend a shape out of its normal form
a part that seems to swell outwards
a repeated pattern that leads the eye

hook.text: How can straight lines on flat paper make it look as if a ball is pushing up through the page?
hook.a: Bend the lines where the ball would be: the brain reads the curves as a raised surface.

starter.q: Which cube face is darkest with light from the top left?
starter.a: The face away from the light (right side).
options: Right side away from the light

starter.a: A smooth change from light to dark.
A strong difference, such as black against white.

teach.heading: The regular grid
teach.note: Start every warped design from a calm grid.

teach.heading: Warping the grid
bullets: Draw a circle where the bulge will be
Inside it, curve the lines outwards
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: Make a bulge in a line grid.
steps: Draw a light circle in the middle
Inside the circle, curve each line upwards like a hill
Rub out the circle; ink the lines
model.answer: Lines that seem to rise over a hidden ball

teach.heading: Black and white
bullets: Fill alternate stripes or squares black
teach.note: Show a black and white chequer bulge (Vasarely-style).

teach.heading: Contour link
teach.note: A map's contours show hills with line spacing, just like our grid.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: To make a bulge, the lines inside the circle should...
check.why: Curved lines following an imagined ball tell the brain the surface rises.

practice.q: Draw a small grid of horizontal lines with one bulge.
practice.a: Lines curving over a circle area.
practice.model: Teacher follows the model slide on a 10 cm square.

independent.q: Core: Make an A4 warped grid design with at least one bulge, inked in black fine liner.
independent.a: An accurate warped grid with a convincing bulge.
independent.model: Teacher rules the grid and places the circle.

independent.q: Extend: Fill alternate sections black to increase the contrast.
independent.a: A black and white design where the bulge stands out.

exit.q: Warping a grid means... A) erasing it B) bending its lines C) colouring it red
exit.a: B) bending its lines

exit.q: Big question: how do straight lines on flat paper make a ball seem to push up?
exit.a: Curving the lines over the ball's area makes the brain read a raised surface.

lessons.homework: Design a second warped grid with a hollow (dip) instead of a bulge.
lessons.send: SEND: a printed grid to warp. EAL: grid, curve, bulge. Stretch: two overlapping bulges.

lessons.title: Colour and contrast in illusion
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a red shape on a blue background seem to float in front?
objectives: To understand how colour contrast can make shapes seem to vibrate, advance or recede
successCriteria: All: explain warm colours advance and cool colours recede
Most: use complementary pairs to make edges vibrate
Some: plan a colour scheme that strengthens a line-based illusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: colour, light and the eye's cone cells
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how the eye perceives colour

keywords.def: seem to come forward
seem to go back
a flickering effect where strong colours meet
a colour looks different depending on the colour beside it

hook.text: Why does a red shape on a blue background seem to float in front?
hook.a: Warm colours seem to advance and cool colours to recede, so the red appears closer.

starter.q: To make a bulge, the grid lines...

teach.heading: Advance and recede
teach.note: Show a red square on blue and a blue square on red.

teach.heading: Vibrating edges
teach.note: Red and green stripes; blue and orange stripes.

teach.heading: Simultaneous contrast
teach.note: Show two identical grey squares on black and white.

teach.heading: Model: colour a warped grid
teach.note: Model.

steps: Edge of the bulge: thin orange next to blue
model.answer: The bulge advances and the edge flickers

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which colour usually seems to come forward?
check.why: Warm, bright colours advance; cool and dark colours recede.

practice.q: Colour two squares: red on blue, blue on red. Which square seems nearer?
practice.a: The red square on blue seems nearer.
practice.model: Teacher colours both and holds them up, asking pupils to vote.

independent.q: Core: Make two colour tests of your warped grid: one warm-on-cool, one cool-on-warm. Which illusion is stronger?
independent.a: Two coloured versions with a judgement.
independent.model: Teacher colours the first test from the model.

independent.q: Extend: Write your colour plan for the final piece in the portal response box. Start: 'I will use... because...'
independent.a: For example: I will use warm oranges for the bulge because warm colours advance.

exit.q: Cool colours seem to... A) advance B) recede
exit.a: B) recede

exit.q: Big question: why does red on blue seem to float in front?
exit.a: Warm colours advance and cool colours recede.

lessons.homework: Make a simultaneous contrast test: one colour on three different backgrounds.
lessons.send: SEND: colour test boxes printed. EAL: warm, cool, advance, recede. Stretch: research Vasarely's 'Vega' series and its colour.

lessons.title: Developing a final illusion piece
lessons.bigQuestion: An illusion fails if one line is wobbly. Why does accuracy matter so much in Op art?
objectives: To understand how to develop a final optical illusion piece from tests and plans
successCriteria: All: choose the strongest test and plan a final piece
Most: produce a neat, accurate illusion with deliberate colour or contrast
Some: annotate the piece explaining how each illusion technique works
lessons.smsc: Moral: itqan, doing work with excellence and care

keywords.def: improving an idea through tests and changes
the finished artwork that shows the best of the project
add notes explaining choices
careful, exact work

hook.text: An illusion fails if one line is wobbly. Why does accuracy matter so much in Op art?
hook.a: The trick depends on a perfectly regular pattern; any error breaks the illusion.

starter.q: How do you make a grid bulge?
starter.a: Curve the lines over a circle area.
Size, impossible object, movement, depth or colour.
A colour looks different depending on its neighbour.

teach.heading: Choosing your idea
teach.note: Fewer techniques done well beat many done badly.

teach.heading: Planning the final piece
bullets: Colour or black and white decided
teach.note: Planning checklist.

head: Step
Check
rows: Bulge, warp or impossible shape placed

teach.heading: Model: working accurately
bullets: Ink or colour one section at a time
teach.note: Model.

steps: Mark 1 cm intervals along two edges
Place the bulge circle with a compass
Warp the lines inside, then ink section by section
model.answer: A precise base for the illusion

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Best way to keep an Op art grid even?
check.why: Even spacing is essential for the illusion; measuring keeps it regular.

practice.q: Write your plan in four lines: size, technique, colour, finish.
practice.a: For example: A4; warped grid with a bulge; warm bulge on cool ground; coloured pencil.
practice.model: Teacher writes their own four-line plan.

independent.q: Core: Begin the final piece: rule the grid, place the illusion and start inking or colouring.
independent.model: Teacher works on the first section on camera.

independent.q: Extend: Annotate a photo of your piece in the portal: label each technique and how it tricks the eye.
independent.a: Labels such as 'warped lines suggest a bulge'.

exit.q: Why does accuracy matter in Op art? A) it doesn't B) the illusion depends on a regular pattern C) it uses more ink
exit.a: B) the illusion depends on a regular pattern
options: The illusion depends on a regular pattern

exit.q: Big question: what would break your illusion?
exit.a: An uneven grid or a wobbly line.

lessons.title: Flowers and plants: observational drawing
lessons.bigQuestion: Every flower of the same kind looks alike, yet no two are identical. What does that tell you?

keywords.def: drawing from looking at the real thing
one of the coloured parts of a flower
one part in front of another
different marks to show texture

hook.text: Every flower of the same kind looks alike, yet no two are identical. What does that tell you?
hook.a: Creation has order and endless variety; careful looking reveals it.

islamicLink.text: After describing gardens, crops and palm trees 'watered with one water' yet different in their fruit, Allah says: 'Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason' (Ar-Ra'd 13:4).

misconception.wrong: Drawing every petal the same 'symbol' shape

independent.q: Observational drawing of a real flower or plant: shapes, overlap, tone and two mark-making techniques.
independent.model: The teacher draws the flower's centre on camera.

independent.q: Extend: add a close-up study of one part.

exit.q: Observation means ...
exit.a: drawing what you see

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Every flower of the same kind looks alike, yet no two are identical. What does that tell you?
exit.a: Creation has order and endless variety; careful looking reveals it.
